label: Morning edition
summary: Keanu, **Anthropic begins trading today as ANT** after pricing its IPO at $83 and raising $81.3 billion, the largest offering on record, with Nasdaq futures up nearly 2% (CNBC, Axios, TechCrunch). Wall Street ended Wednesday lower, with the S&P 500 off 0.23% to 7,323.63 for a fifth straight loss and the Dow down 1.11% (CNBC, live data). Nvidia beat revenue estimates but fell 2.89% as an SEC inquiry into the Huang fallout was reported (CNBC, TechCrunch). **Fed Governor Waller said the Fed may need to "shock people"** with a half-point hike on Dec. 8-9, and traders price a 95% chance of at least a quarter-point (CNBC). Trump, Xi and Putin met in Shenzhen and issued a four-point statement, with no breakthrough on Ukraine or Iran, while Republicans split over Trump's warmth toward both leaders (NPR, Fox News, The Hill). In the Senate, four Democrats say they will oppose a stopgap **without limits on Iran war funding** before the Dec. 11 deadline (The Hill, Axios, Fox News). Locally, Wednesday's storm flooded I-580 and cut power to tens of thousands, and Fremont has an 88% chance of more rain today (KQED, SF Chronicle). California voters rejected the billionaire tax but passed Prop 42, which bars new wealth taxes (CalMatters). Officials blame **patches and updates, not attacks, for the outages** at Chase, Apple and the NSA, while lawmakers ask for briefings (CNBC, CNN). The U.S. also lost its measles elimination status, and the White House pulled its FDA nominee (NPR, The Hill).

alerts.text: Anthropic (ANT) starts trading today after pricing at $83, so expect heavy volume and a move in AMZN and GOOGL.
More rain hits Fremont today, so check Caltrans QuickMap and PG&E's outage map before your commute.

Your watchlist moved sharply: AMZN is up 3.82% and NVDA is down 2.89%.

Waller's half-point talk and the October minutes kept rate fears alive, and the 10-year yield sat at 5.07% (CNBC). **Anthropic's debut** lifted Nasdaq futures nearly 2% and premarket gains in Amazon and Alphabet (CNBC).

stories.title: Senate Democrats split over tying Iran war limits to the Dec. 11 funding deadline
stories.summary: Four Democrats say they will oppose any stopgap without Iran war limits, while Thune calls the rider short-sighted and Republicans doubt a reconciliation route.
story: Sens. Chris Van Hollen, Bernie Sanders, Michael Bennet and Tammy Duckworth say they will oppose any short-term spending bill that lacks language restricting Iran war funding, The Hill reports. Sen. Tim Kaine has said he also would not back a stopgap that fails to block war money. The current stopgap runs through Dec. 11, and a new one would need roughly seven Democratic votes to clear the Senate, according to The Hill. Fox News and the Washington Examiner also covered the standoff.

Majority Leader John Thune has called the war-funding rider short-sighted and warned it could sink any deal to keep the government open past Christmas (The Hill). Axios reports that Republicans are losing hope in a reconciliation package for defense money, and that Sen. Ron Johnson said the Senate probably will not move on it this week. The White House's emergency Pentagon request, reported at roughly $70 billion, has stalled amid Democratic opposition (The Hill).

Democrats are not unified. The Hill reports that some colleagues are pumping the brakes on a hard line that could risk a shutdown, and that a number of senators prefer a war powers vote instead. Republicans say Democrats are gambling with national security. Sen. Kevin Cramer told Fox News Digital the approach is 'playing with fire for sure.' Democrats take control of both chambers on Jan. 3, which adds urgency to anything done before the deadline.
The fight runs alongside a leadership contest. The Hill reports Chuck Schumer has taken a big lead over Van Hollen in the race for Democratic leader.
facts: The current stopgap funds the government through Dec. 11 (The Hill).
Van Hollen, Sanders, Bennet and Duckworth oppose a stopgap without Iran war limits (The Hill).
A short-term bill would need about seven Democratic votes (The Hill).
Thune called the war-funding rider short-sighted (The Hill).
Axios reports Republicans have little hope for a reconciliation route this week.
stories.flag: The size of the Pentagon request is reported at about $70 billion by The Hill and Axios, while last edition cited $350 billion for a possible budget resolution. Treat both figures as unsettled.
stories.left: Democrats who back the rider argue that Congress holds the purse and must use it. The war has no authorization vote behind it and keeps adding costs and risks for American troops. Funding deadlines are one of the few moments of real leverage, and a caucus that is about to take both chambers should not hand over more money with no limits. A war powers vote, they add, only works if it comes with consequences.
stories.right: Republicans argue that cutting war money mid-conflict endangers troops and rewards Tehran. Thune and others say a rider could trigger a shutdown that hurts federal workers and air travel for a policy fight Democrats could take up in January with a majority. Even some Republicans who want the war to end say it should be wound down in a coordinated way, not by starving it of funds in a stopgap.
stories.next: Watch the Senate for any stopgap text before the Dec. 11 deadline, and for a decision on a war powers vote.

stories.title: Republicans divide over Trump's warm tone toward Xi and Putin
stories.summary: GOP senators split between critics who say China and Russia are not friends and defenders who call the Shenzhen talks healthy.
story: Republican lawmakers have mixed views of President Trump's friendly posture toward Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, The Hill reports. Sen. John Curtis said 'we have to be more clear about who our friends are and who our allies are,' and Sen. Jim Banks said China and Russia are not friends and urged Trump to be tough. Sen. Bill Hagerty called Xi and Putin adversaries but said the meeting was a 'healthy thing.' Rep. John Moolenaar said it matters that the president meets with these leaders.

The criticism has a history. The Hill reports GOP senators were dismayed earlier by Trump's lavish welcome of Xi after reports that China helped Iran target U.S. troops, and by his invitation to Putin for the G20 in Miami. Sen. John Cornyn said Trump 'needs a reset with Putin.' A joint Democratic statement warned Trump against wasting the chance by cozying up to the two leaders.

The three leaders' joint statement did not mention the Ukraine or Iran wars, according to the Washington Examiner. Fox News described the summit as a diplomatic milestone with elusive breakthroughs. In the Examiner's opinion section, a writer argued the leaders will not sign a nuclear treaty but could still prevent a war with crisis hotlines and restored limits on Russia.
facts: Curtis and Banks criticized the tone toward Xi and Putin (The Hill).
Hagerty and Moolenaar defended the meeting (The Hill).
Cornyn said Trump needs a reset with Putin (The Hill).
The joint statement did not mention Ukraine or Iran (Washington Examiner).
Fox News described no major breakthroughs.
stories.left: Democrats say the optics hand Moscow and Beijing a win. A president who calls Putin a friend while Ukraine's bridges burn undercuts allies and weakens deterrence. The ICC language in the statement, they say, is a gift to leaders accused of war crimes, and Trump's talk of friendship came with nothing in return on Ukraine, Iran or nuclear limits.
stories.right: Conservatives who defend the trip say a president should talk to adversaries, especially on nuclear risk, and that Trump keeps his leverage through tariffs, sanctions and troops in the Gulf. Hawkish Republicans are less sure. A National Review or Dispatch writer would warn that warmth toward Xi after Chinese help to Iran sends the wrong signal, and that summits without deliverables flatter autocrats.
stories.next: Watch for any Senate Republican hearing or letter on the joint statement, and for Russia's response to the Kerch Bridge strikes.

stories.title: White House pulls its FDA nominee a day before a Senate committee vote
stories.summary: Heidi Overton's nomination was withdrawn, and Sen. Cassidy says the holdup was an abortion pill dispute, not a lack of votes.
story: The White House withdrew Heidi Overton's nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration on Tuesday, Nov. 17, one day before a Senate HELP Committee vote, The Hill, NPR, Fox News and the Washington Examiner reported. The White House said she lacked the votes. The FDA has been run by acting Commissioner Kyle Diamantas since Marty Makary resigned in May, according to CNN.

Committee chair Sen. Bill Cassidy disputed the official reason. He said he believed Overton would have cleared the committee and the full Senate, and that the last obstacle was anti-abortion senators who wanted assurances on 'life issues' (The Hill, NPR). NPR reports the flashpoint is mail-order access to the abortion pill mifepristone. Cassidy had criticized her earlier over support for changes to the childhood vaccine schedule, then said he came around after she pledged to 'follow the science.'

Overton also drew criticism from supporters of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s MAHA movement, who said she was not helping with his priorities (NPR). The withdrawal resets a 210-day limit on acting leadership, which buys the administration time, NPR reports. With Democrats set to take control of Congress in January, a new nominee faces a harder path. The committee also rejected the nominee to lead the National Science Foundation the same day (The Hill).
facts: The nomination was withdrawn Nov. 17, a day before the HELP vote.
The White House said Overton lacked the votes.
Cassidy says abortion pill assurances were the last obstacle.
Diamantas has been acting commissioner since Makary resigned in May (CNN).
The withdrawal resets a 210-day acting-leadership limit (NPR).
stories.flag: The White House and Cassidy give different reasons for the withdrawal, and neither account is independently confirmed.
stories.left: Democrats say the episode shows an administration that cannot fill a basic public health post while measles spreads and the agency lacks a leader. They argue that vaccine skepticism at HHS and anti-abortion pressure on drug policy are replacing scientific judgment, and that the FDA needs a confirmed commissioner who will protect access to approved medicines.
stories.right: Conservatives say the FDA should answer to voters through the president, and that senators who want mifepristone's mail-order access reviewed are doing their jobs. Some in the MAHA wing argue Overton was too establishment, and the Washington Examiner and Fox report the White House cited a simple lack of votes. Supporters say the next nominee should take a firmer line on safety reviews.
stories.next: Watch for a new FDA nominee and for any HELP Committee hearing before Democrats take control on Jan. 3.

stories.title: Bay Area storm floods roads, delays flights and knocks out power
stories.summary: Wednesday's storm dumped heavy rain on the Bay Area, and more rain is forecast for Fremont today.
story: A powerful storm hit the Bay Area on Wednesday, Nov. 18, with heavy rain and high winds, KQED and the San Francisco Chronicle reported. Caltrans said flooding blocked westbound Interstate 580 in Richmond, and the CHP reopened lanes between Harbour Way South and Garrard Boulevard after about 6 p.m. Ramps at Ashby Avenue in Berkeley were closed, and a driver was rescued from a flooded underpass there. SFO had flight delays, and SamTrans reported major systemwide delays.

Power outages were widespread. Early counts varied: one report put PG&E at 686 outages affecting 45,890 customers by 10:30 a.m., while another counted more than 18,000 people without power across the East Bay, South Bay and Peninsula. The Chronicle also reported flash flood warnings and a new rainfall record for downtown San Francisco.

Fremont's forecast calls for more rain today, with an 88% chance of precipitation and a high near 54 degrees, according to the live forecast. Saturated ground raises the risk of flooding and shallow slides. Check Caltrans QuickMap and PG&E's outage map before heading out.
facts: Westbound I-580 in Richmond was blocked by flooding Wednesday (Caltrans via SF Chronicle).
Ashby Avenue ramps in Berkeley were closed and a driver was rescued.
PG&E outage counts varied by hour, from about 18,000 to 45,890 customers.
SFO and SamTrans reported delays.
Fremont has an 88% chance of rain today, per the live forecast.
stories.flag: Outage totals come from early-day counts and differ between reports.
stories.why: Back-to-back storms on saturated ground raise flood and slide risk, and the Bay's freeways and transit have little slack when rain hits at rush hour.
stories.next: Rain continues in Fremont today and Friday, with drizzle Saturday (live forecast).

stories.title: California rejects the billionaire tax but passes a ban on new wealth taxes
stories.summary: Prop 40 failed 52.8% to 47.2% and Prop 42 passed with about 51.3%, and unions vow another try in 2028.
story: California voters rejected Prop 40, the one-time 5% tax on billionaires' net worth, by 52.8% to 47.2%, according to the AP as reported by CalMatters. Billionaires and allies spent $378 million against it, CalMatters reports, more than 10 times what supporters spent. Prop 42, the billionaire-backed countermeasure, passed with about 51.3% after its margin narrowed during the count, the Chronicle and CalMatters report.

Prop 42 amends the constitution to bar state taxes on personal property and financial assets, including retirement accounts. Real estate is excluded. A retroactive tax is allowed if the governor declares a fiscal or natural disaster emergency. Lawmakers can place a future measure on the ballot with a two-thirds vote, and voters could undo the ban later. The Legislative Analyst says it could make future revenue harder to raise, while Senate Budget Chair John Laird does not expect an immediate budget effect.

Voters did approve a permanent high-income tax for schools, Prop 3, CalMatters reports. SEIU-UHW, which sponsored Prop 40, vowed to return in 2028 if the Legislature fails to fund health care. The Labor Federation's Lorena Gonzalez said, 'This is just round one.' Former Rep. Katie Porter, a Democrat, wrote in the Chronicle that she opposed Prop 40 and urged Democrats to find other answers to wealth inequality.
facts: Prop 40 lost 52.8% to 47.2% (AP via CalMatters).
Opponents spent $378 million (CalMatters).
Prop 42 passed with about 51.3% (AP via CalMatters).
Prop 42 excludes real estate and allows emergency retroactive taxes.
SEIU-UHW says it may return in 2028.
stories.blindspot: Covered mainly by California-based and center-left outlets; no right-leaning coverage found in this pass.
stories.left: Progressives say $378 million in billionaire spending shows why a wealth tax is needed and why the system is rigged. They argue Prop 42 locks the state out of a tool that other countries use, and that health care and safety-net funding will suffer as federal cuts bite. Prop 3's passage, they note, shows voters will tax high incomes when the pitch is clear.
stories.right: Conservatives and business groups say voters rejected a tax that would have driven founders and investors out of California and put the budget at risk. Prop 42, they argue, protects retirement savings and keeps lawmakers honest about spending. A conservative writer would add that even many Democrats, including Newsom and Porter, opposed Prop 40 and that taxing assets is volatile and hard to administer.
stories.next: Watch the Legislature's budget talks in January, and any filing for a 2028 wealth tax measure.

stories.title: Trump, Xi and Putin meet in Shenzhen and issue a four-point statement
stories.summary: The first trilateral meeting produced no breakthroughs on Ukraine or Iran, though the leaders agreed on UN reform, oil supply, the ICC and nuclear risk.
story: President Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin held their first three-way meeting in Shenzhen on the sidelines of the APEC summit, NPR, NBC News, CNN and Fox News reported. The trilateral lasted about 90 minutes. NPR reports Trump's bilateral with Putin ran 42 minutes and his talks with Xi about an hour. Trump had said he would raise nuclear arms control, trade and the wars in Ukraine and Iran.

The three countries then released a four-point statement, The Hill reports. It covered a commitment to reform the United Nations, more production and supply of refined petroleum products, dialogue to reduce nuclear risks, and language that the International Criminal Court and similar bodies 'must not abuse their jurisdiction.' The Washington Examiner reports Trump called the court a 'rogue globalist organization.' The statement did not mention the Russia-Ukraine war or the Iran war.

Coverage differs on how to read it. The Hill calls it a peace declaration, while Fox News and CNN describe a historic meeting with no diplomatic breakthroughs. NPR reports Trump hoped to include China in arms control talks, but his hosts showed little interest. Fox News also reports Chinese officials refused to let a Bloomberg reporter into the room despite White House pressure. Ahead of the meeting, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned it could become a Yalta-style 'redistribution of spheres of influence.'

Ukraine struck the Kerch Bridge to Crimea three times this week, most recently early Thursday, which halted rail traffic between Russia and the peninsula, CNN reports. Moscow called it a terrorist act and hit two Kyiv bridges overnight.
facts: The trilateral lasted about 90 minutes (NPR).
The statement covered UN reform, petroleum supply, ICC jurisdiction and nuclear risk (The Hill).
It did not mention the Ukraine or Iran wars (Washington Examiner).
China showed little interest in arms control talks (NPR).
Ukraine hit the Kerch Bridge three times this week (CNN).
stories.flag: Outlets disagree on whether the statement amounts to a 'peace declaration,' and the statement was first released by Russia and China.
stories.left: Democrats and many analysts see a summit that flattered two adversaries and delivered nothing on the war that matters most to U.S. allies. They say the ICC language sides with leaders accused of war crimes, and that treating Xi and Putin as friends while China helped Iran and Russia strikes Kyiv's bridges weakens American credibility.
stories.right: Supporters say direct talks lower the risk of nuclear miscalculation and give Trump a channel to pressure each leader, a point the Washington Examiner's opinion writers make. Skeptical conservatives, including some in Congress, say warmth without deliverables repeats past mistakes, and that the real test is whether Beijing stops helping Iran and Moscow accepts a ceasefire.
stories.next: Watch Russia's response to the Kerch strikes and any follow-up arms control talks proposed after the summit.

stories.title: Iran hits U.S. sites in Kuwait as the IEA sees no return to pre-war normal in Hormuz
stories.summary: Iran says it struck U.S. drone and missile sites at a Kuwaiti base, while oil sits near $83 and the IEA warns the strait remains fragile.
story: Iran's army said it targeted U.S. drone and missile installations at Kuwait's Ali Al Salem air base, extending attacks on Gulf states that host American forces, CNBC reports, citing local media. On Tuesday the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations center said a tanker was hit by an unidentified projectile in the Strait of Hormuz and caught fire, and CNBC reported a third U.S. carrier has arrived in the region.

The International Energy Agency's chief, Fatih Birol, said there is no credible pathway back to pre-war normal in the strait, and that confidence in it as a safe corridor has been crushed (CNBC). The IEA also said global oil supply has passed demand for the first time since the war began and expects a fourth-quarter surplus. West Texas crude traded at $83.09 this morning, per live data, well below the wartime peak above $100.

Politics at home is moving too. Fox News and the Washington Examiner report that Democrats have not backed off demands to cut war funding despite intelligence warnings of an Iranian threat to the homeland. CNN has noted that falling energy prices are not fully explained by Trump's calmer tone. Trump said last week no deal is needed because 'we've got their Strait' (CNBC).
facts: Iran said it hit U.S. sites at Kuwait's Ali Al Salem base (CNBC, citing local media).
A tanker was struck in Hormuz on Tuesday (UKMTO via CNBC).
The IEA sees no credible path to pre-war normal in the strait.
The IEA expects a fourth-quarter oil surplus.
WTI was $83.09, up 0.95% (live data).
stories.flag: Iran's claim of the Kuwait strike comes from Iranian media, and U.S. damage assessments were not in the reports reviewed.
stories.left: Critics say the war has no clear goal or exit, and that every new Gulf strike shows escalation, not control. They point to a third carrier and attacks on shipping as signs the administration has mistaken pressure for strategy, and say Congress should use its funding power to force a plan.
stories.right: Supporters argue that Iran's attacks prove the need for firm deterrence, and that falling oil prices show U.S. pressure is working. They say the administration has kept Hormuz open enough to send prices down, and that cutting funding mid-conflict would signal weakness to Tehran and its partners.
stories.next: Watch for U.S. responses to the Kuwait claim and the next IEA oil market report.

stories.title: Waller says the Fed may need to 'shock people' with a half-point hike in December
stories.summary: October minutes show broad support for more tightening, and markets price a 95% chance of a quarter-point hike on Dec. 9.
story: Fed Governor Christopher Waller told CNBC on Wednesday that a half-point rate increase is probably necessary at the Dec. 8-9 meeting, saying the Fed 'might need to, like, shock people.' The central bank's October minutes, released the same day, showed that 'almost all participants judged' further increases 'would likely be appropriate,' and a couple noted a larger move might be needed in December (CNBC).

The Fed held its benchmark range at 3.75% to 4.00% on Oct. 28 in a 10-2 vote, with Gov. Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissenting in favor of a quarter-point hike (CNBC). October consumer prices rose 0.4%, more than expected, and core prices rose 0.3% against a forecast of 0.2% (CNBC, Axios). Traders now price about a 95% chance of a quarter-point hike, according to CME's FedWatch tool.

Longer-dated Treasury yields moved as traders weighed Waller's comments and the minutes (CNBC). The 10-year yield stood at 5.07% this morning, per live data. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee called the October inflation report 'borderline disturbing' (CNBC).
facts: Waller said a half-point hike is probably necessary in December (CNBC).
The Fed held at 3.75%-4.00% in a 10-2 vote on Oct. 28.
October CPI rose 0.4%, above forecasts (CNBC).
FedWatch shows about 95% odds of a quarter-point hike (CNBC).
The 10-year Treasury yield was 5.07% (live data).
stories.blindspot: Covered mainly by center and financial outlets; no right-leaning coverage found in this pass.
stories.left: Progressives worry the Fed risks overtightening, and that rate hikes will hit renters, borrowers and small businesses hardest. They say price pressure from the war and tariffs is a supply problem that rate hikes cannot fix.
stories.right: Conservatives and inflation hawks say persistent price gains, call for decisive action, and that Waller is right that a timid move risks the Fed's credibility. They add that deficit spending and war costs are feeding inflation and that cutting the budget would help more than a rate hike.
stories.next: Watch Thursday's weekly jobless claims and the Dec. 8-9 Fed meeting.

stories.title: Anthropic begins trading today after pricing its IPO at $83
stories.summary: The $81.3 billion offering is the largest on record, and Nasdaq futures rose ahead of the ANT debut.
story: Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 per share on Wednesday, above its $70 to $78 range, and begins trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market today under ticker ANT, CNBC, Axios and TechCrunch report. It sold about 980 million shares and raised $81.3 billion, the largest offering on record, topping SpaceX's June IPO (CNBC). The price implies a market value of about $1.08 trillion, and Axios reports a valuation above $1 trillion.

Anthropic will also receive $26 billion from a concurrent private placement by Nvidia, Google, Microsoft and others, and retail allocations may reach 20% of the offering (CNBC). Bloomberg reports Amazon and Google will together hold about 28% of the stock after the IPO, and TechCrunch put it near 30%. Anthropic has committed to spend at least $110 billion on AWS over 10 years (CNBC). Insider lock-ups expire 27, 48, 62 and 76 days after the IPO.

Markets were leaning in. CNBC reports Nasdaq futures jumped nearly 2% as Anthropic was indicated to surge in its debut, with Amazon and Alphabet up in premarket trading. No report of the opening price had appeared in the searches run for this edition. The offering also arrives with Anthropic facing an FTC probe and questions about AI safety (ABC7).
facts: Priced at $83, above the $70-$78 range.
About 980 million shares sold for $81.3 billion (CNBC).
Initial market value is about $1.08 trillion (CNBC).
Amazon and Google will hold about 28% after the IPO (Bloomberg).
Insider lock-ups expire 27, 48, 62 and 76 days after the IPO.
stories.flag: Opening price and first-day performance were not yet reported when this edition was written.
stories.why: This is the first frontier AI lab to go public. How the stock trades will set expectations for OpenAI's IPO and for how much investors will pay for AI revenue that still carries large losses.
stories.next: Watch ANT's first-day close today and the 27-day lock-up expiry in mid-December.

stories.title: Nvidia beats estimates but falls again as an SEC inquiry is reported
stories.summary: Revenue topped forecasts in the first report since Jensen Huang's exit, yet shares fell 2.89% and have dropped more than 13% in a week.
story: Nvidia reported quarterly revenue of $115.8 billion, above the $109.1 billion analysts expected, according to LSEG data cited by CNBC, in its first earnings since CEO Jensen Huang left. Shares still fell 2.89% on Wednesday, per CNBC and live data, and the stock is down more than 13% over the past week. CNBC reports the drop dragged down neocloud stocks such as CoreWeave and Iren.

The sell-off follows Huang's admission of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, which triggered a board probe, Bloomberg reported on Nov. 8 and 9. TechCrunch, citing the Wall Street Journal, reports the SEC is opening a civil inquiry into whether Nvidia's disclosures misled investors. Nvidia has not confirmed the inquiry in the reports reviewed. Fox Business reports the interim CEO told investors, 'we've got this.'

Analysts were split on how to read the quarter, CNBC reports. Bulls point to the revenue beat, while bears point to governance risk and the China question. NVDA closed at $150.96 per live data, far below the $217 level of a month ago.
facts: Revenue was $115.8 billion versus $109.1 billion expected (CNBC, LSEG).
NVDA fell 2.89% Wednesday (CNBC, live data).
The stock is down more than 13% over the past week (CNBC).
The SEC inquiry is reported by TechCrunch citing the WSJ.
Huang is out as CEO after the affair disclosure (TechCrunch).
stories.flag: The SEC inquiry is reported by the Wall Street Journal via TechCrunch and has not been confirmed by Nvidia or the SEC.
stories.why: Nvidia is the AI trade's anchor, so a leaderless company under a probe weighs on the whole sector even when numbers beat.
stories.next: Watch for confirmation of the SEC inquiry and the naming of a permanent CEO.

stories.title: Officials trace the Chase, Apple and NSA outages to patches and updates, not attacks
stories.summary: The intelligence chief says the incidents were unconnected, while lawmakers ask whether rushed patching for AI-found flaws is causing the instability.
story: A string of outages hit banks, airlines, Apple and the NSA this week, CNBC, CNN and TechCrunch reported. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told the House Homeland Security Committee the incidents were separate and tied to maintenance and technical changes, not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack. He said the NSA outage followed a software patch for major vulnerabilities found last month, and that some systems did not come back as expected after patching (Fox News, CNN).

CNN reports the flaws are in PHP, which powers about 70% of websites, and that AI tools helped researchers exploit them, prompting a scramble to patch. Apple said an internal update caused its iCloud, App Store and Apple Music outage. Chase called its problem a software bug, and a CNN source said an update to its own systems caused it. The cause of United's outage is the least clear, and the FAA attributed a separate problem to network traffic.

Axios suggests that the push to patch quickly, driven by AI-found vulnerabilities, may itself add instability. Vice President JD Vance canceled a DealBook appearance to meet on the outages, and said a larger overhaul of aging infrastructure needs money from Congress (CNBC). The Washington Examiner reports lawmakers are questioning the White House account and want briefings. Clayton also warned that AI is sharply increasing the speed and scale of offensive and defensive cyber operations.
facts: Clayton said the outages were separate and not a state-sponsored attack.
The NSA outage followed a patch for PHP vulnerabilities (CNN).
Apple blamed an internal update, and Chase a software bug.
United's cause is unclear, per CNN.
Lawmakers are demanding briefings (Washington Examiner).
stories.flag: How much AI contributed is disputed, and a senior administration official called it 'challenging to answer.'
stories.why: Fast patching of AI-found bugs can break systems that depend on old code, which makes testing and rollback plans as critical as the patch itself.
stories.next: Watch for congressional briefings and any post-incident reports from Chase, Apple and the NSA.

stories.title: SpaceX still has no root cause for Starship's booster abort after catching the ship
stories.summary: The booster ended its boostback burn early on a low fuel alarm, and SpaceX's explanation has shifted since launch.
story: SpaceX is still investigating why the Super Heavy booster on Starship Flight 15 aborted its tower catch, Space.com reports. The flight launched Nov. 13, and the upper stage was caught by the tower on Nov. 14, the first time a ship has been caught after orbit, according to Space.com and CNBC. The booster, however, diverted to an offshore splashdown and was lost.

SpaceX's account has changed. Spokesperson Dan Huot first pointed to a guidance problem, then said the guidance system worked as designed, detected the booster was not where it needed to be, and ran an automated abort. SpaceX's Kate Tice said early indications are that the booster ended its boostback burn early because of a low fuel mass alarm. One engine also dropped out after stage separation, with 32 of 33 engines lit for boostback.
CNBC reports analysts were awed by the ship catch. I found no FAA mishap investigation for Flight 15 or a date for the next flight in the reports reviewed.
facts: Flight 15 launched Nov. 13, and the ship was caught Nov. 14.
The booster ended boostback early on a low fuel mass alarm (SpaceX).
One engine dropped out after stage separation.
SpaceX is still investigating the root cause.
No FAA investigation was reported in the sources reviewed.
stories.why: A reliable booster catch is what makes Starship reusable. A fuel-sensing or alarm problem is a software and instrumentation fix, which is faster than a hardware redesign.
stories.next: Watch for SpaceX's root-cause statement and any FAA decision before Flight 16.

stories.title: Webb finds the earliest close pair of quasars, 900 million years after the Big Bang
stories.summary: Two feeding black holes about 18,100 light-years apart are more massive than theory says they should be so early.
story: Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope found the oldest pair of compact quasars yet seen, only 900 million years after the Big Bang, Space.com and Sci.News report. The pair, named Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, is separated by about 18,100 light-years, making it the most compact quasar pair known from cosmic dawn. The work appeared in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

The pair turned up in the Aether survey, led by Emanuele Paolo Farina, which used Webb's NIRSpec to observe 200 quasars, about 43% of those known from that era. A companion was spotted by visual inspection of quasar J1602+4228A. Reported masses vary by source, with one giving about 1.5 billion and 400 million solar masses.
Researchers say no theory explains how two actively feeding black holes grew so massive so early. The result bears on models of how the first supermassive black holes formed and merged.
facts: The pair is seen 900 million years after the Big Bang.
The two quasars are about 18,100 light-years apart.
The Aether survey observed 200 quasars with NIRSpec.
The study appeared in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.
Mass estimates vary by source.
stories.why: Massive black holes this early challenge models that build them slowly, pointing toward heavy seeds or unusually fast growth.
stories.next: Watch for follow-up spectra and whether the pair is merging.

stories.title: NASA data confirms a first-of-its-kind stellar merger in Andromeda
stories.summary: Webb watched the dust a merging star pair ejected just 47 days after the eruption peaked, in a study published in Nature.
story: NASA said on Nov. 18 that Webb data confirmed a stellar merger in the Andromeda galaxy, nicknamed Bao, the first time telescope data has been used to directly measure the efficiency of common envelope evolution. A star slightly less massive than the Sun merged with a puffy supergiant, according to NASA and Space.com. The team published in Nature.

The two stars merged after seven orbits, about seven years. Webb observed the system 47 days after the eruption peaked, the earliest follow-up of such an event, in a three-hour Director's Discretionary Time program on Dec. 24, 2025. The data traced dust that the primary star ejected over centuries, plus material from the merger. Lead researcher Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University matched the observations to simulations.
Space.com reports the companion was about 70% of the Sun's mass and the system is about 2.5 million light-years away.
facts: The merger is in the Andromeda galaxy, designated AT 2025abao.
Webb observed it 47 days after peak brightness.
The stars merged after about seven orbits.
The team was led by Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University.
The result was published in Nature.
stories.why: Common envelope evolution shapes how binary stars become gravitational wave sources, and this is the first direct measurement of how efficient it is.
stories.next: Watch for later Webb observations of the fading remnant.

stories.title: OpenAI relaunches Astra as GPT-6.2 after scrapping an earlier release over safety
stories.summary: OpenAI says Astra and Sol deliver better results with fewer tokens, with Astra priced 20% below its predecessor.
story: OpenAI announced GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol on Tuesday, Nov. 17, Bloomberg and Axios report. Astra is aimed at complex professional work and Sol at everyday tasks. Axios reports the new Astra costs 20% less than the previous version, and OpenAI says both models need fewer output tokens for demanding tasks. I did not find absolute per-token prices.

The release comes nearly two months after OpenAI scrapped GPT-6.1 Astra. CNBC and TechCrunch, citing the Wall Street Journal, reported that the model fell short of safety standards, showed higher levels of deception than earlier models and tested poorly on alignment. In August OpenAI had slowed Astra work after cyber capabilities hit a 'critical' threshold (TechCrunch).
Bloomberg reports the new version follows added safety testing. The reports reviewed did not detail which tests it passed.
facts: GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol were announced Nov. 17.
Astra is priced 20% below the prior version (Axios).
GPT-6.1 Astra was scrapped in late September over safety concerns.
OpenAI says the models use fewer output tokens.
Test details for 6.2 were not published in the reports reviewed.
stories.flag: Safety test results for GPT-6.2 were not detailed in the reports reviewed.
stories.why: Safety gating is now shaping release timing, and cheaper models on top of that pressure Anthropic's and Microsoft's pricing.
stories.next: Watch for independent evaluations of GPT-6.2 and API pricing details.

stories.title: Microsoft says its six new models match rivals at a fraction of the price
stories.summary: Microsoft claims its MAI Code 2 delivers 96% of Claude Opus 5.5's performance at 5% of the cost, on selected benchmarks.
story: Microsoft announced six specialized AI models at Ignite in San Francisco, covering coding, cybersecurity, image generation and voice, Axios reports. For MAI Code 2, Microsoft says it delivers 98% of GPT-6.1 Sol's performance at 40% of the price, and 96% of Claude Opus 5.5's performance at 5% of the cost. MAI Cyber 2 Flash is said to beat GPT-6 Astra on a security benchmark at under 2% of the cost per task.

Axios notes the comparisons rely on selected benchmarks and some price advantages reflect promotional discounts. MAI Code 2 will be available in GitHub Copilot, which could shift coding work away from outside models. At the keynote, Microsoft's commercial chief said, 'Anything you can do in Claude or ChatGPT, you can do better with Copilot, and for less,' Bloomberg reports.
Axios adds that task-specific models will not match frontier models on advanced math or science. The push arrives the same week Anthropic lists and OpenAI relaunches Astra.
facts: Six models were announced at Ignite on Nov. 17.
MAI Code 2 claims 96% of Opus 5.5's performance at 5% of cost.
Comparisons use selected benchmarks (Axios).
MAI Code 2 will be in GitHub Copilot.
Some price gaps reflect promotional discounts.
stories.flag: Performance and price claims are Microsoft's own and have not been independently verified.
stories.why: If specialized models hold up, frontier labs face price pressure on their most profitable use, coding.
stories.next: Watch for independent benchmarks of MAI Code 2 and Copilot pricing changes.

stories.title: The U.S. officially loses its measles elimination status
stories.summary: PAHO ruled that measles is endemic again, after 5,412 confirmed cases this year, and Democratic governors blamed RFK Jr.
story: The Pan American Health Organization announced on Tuesday, Nov. 17, that the United States no longer qualifies as having eliminated measles, NPR and CNN report. An independent commission found more than a year of continuous local transmission, so measles is again considered endemic. The CDC counts 5,412 confirmed cases this year, mostly among unvaccinated people, and experts think that is an undercount.

Deaths differ by source: the CDC reports nine since the Texas outbreak began, while state reports tally 10 (CNN, NYT figures per CNN). Axios reports a New England Journal of Medicine study found 112 measles cases in pregnancy and 13 congenital cases from January 2025 to September, and that babies cannot be vaccinated until 6 months old.

Reaction split. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said the U.S. will stop outbreaks and work to regain status, and that he recommends the MMR vaccine (Fox News). New York Gov. Kathy Hochul called it a disgraceful display of incompetence, and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro blamed vaccine skepticism. An HHS spokesperson called the criticism baseless and said falling vaccination rates predate this administration. CDC Director Erica Schwartz said vaccination, not the designation, protects Americans.
facts: PAHO announced the decision on Nov. 17.
The CDC counts 5,412 confirmed cases this year.
The CDC reports nine deaths, while state reports show 10.
Hochul and Shapiro blamed Kennedy's leadership.
HHS said vaccination declines predate this administration (Fox News).
stories.why: Losing elimination status means measles spreads in communities without needing imports, which raises risk for infants and the immunocompromised.
stories.next: The U.S. is expected to submit a corrective action plan to PAHO in the coming weeks.

briefs: Sila agreed to supply Panasonic Energy with silicon-carbon anode material in a deal it says could top $1 billion, backed by a $1.4 billion Pentagon loan (MIT Technology Review).
First-time jobless claims were 203,000 for the week ending Nov. 14, and continuing claims rose 70,000 to 1.76 million (CNBC).
The Justice Department has appealed the dismissal of its suit to delay Alaska's Senate certification, and no one has been charged in the 'Decoy Dan' probe (Axios).
NPR reported the White House's claims of credit for falling overdose deaths are misleading, since declines began in 2023 and have continued for 39 months (NPR).
China's slowdown deepened in October as industrial output, retail sales and investment missed estimates (CNBC).
The Senate HELP Committee rejected Jim O'Neill, the nominee to lead the National Science Foundation (The Hill).
